Inspiration of Scripture
in-spuh-RAY-shuhn uhv SKRIP-chur
doctrinal phrase
From Latin inspirare (to breathe into), rendering Paul's Greek theopneustos (God-breathed); inspiration is the act by which God breathed out His Word through chosen men.

See also: Inspiration of Scripture

Biblical Definition

The inspiration of Scripture is that supernatural work whereby God so superintended the human authors of the Bible that, using their own minds, styles, and circumstances, they wrote without error the very words God intended—so that the product is in truth the Word of God. Paul states it directly: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God," literally God-breathed, theopneustos, exhaled from the mouth of God Himself. Peter unfolds the manner: "the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost," borne along as a ship is carried by the wind. This is verbal plenary inspiration: verbal, because it extends to the very words and not merely the thoughts; plenary, because it reaches every part, from Genesis to Revelation, equally and fully. Such inspiration secures inerrancy—the Scriptures, in their original autographs, are without error in all they affirm—and undergirds sola scriptura, that the Bible alone is the supreme and sufficient rule of faith and life. The men were not passive pens, yet neither were they free authors; the Spirit moved them so that what they wrote, God said. The 1689 Confession confesses the Holy Scripture to be "given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life." To receive the Bible as God-breathed is to bow to its every word as to the voice of the living God, who cannot lie and does not err.

Webster 1828 Definition

The supernatural influence of the Spirit of God upon the writers of Scripture, by which they were qualified to communicate divine truth without error; the quality of being God-breathed.

INSPIRATION, n. From Latin inspirare, to breathe into; the act of breathing in.

The infusion of ideas or supernatural influence into the mind by the Spirit of God.

The communication of divine truth to the sacred writers, such that what they wrote is the very word of God.

Paul's testimony: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine" (2Ti 3:16).

The God-breathed quality of Holy Scripture, extending to its very words and to all its parts.

Key Scripture

2Ti 3:16 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness."

2Pe 1:21 — "For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost."

2Pe 1:20 — "Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation."

Joh 10:35 — "If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken."

Modern Corruption

The historical-critical method denies that Scripture is God-breathed, reducing it to a merely human record of evolving religion and dissolving its inerrant authority.

expand to see more

The reigning corruption is the historical-critical denial of inspiration, which treats the Bible as a purely human collection of religious literature—layered, edited, and contradictory—rather than the God-breathed Word. On this view, "inspiration" means at most that the writers were religiously gifted men, and the text records their evolving ideas about God rather than God's own self-revelation. Stripped of its divine authorship, Scripture becomes an artifact to be dissected rather than a voice to be obeyed, and the believer is left to sift the "authentic" from the "legendary" by the shifting standards of the critic.

The principle to recover is verbal plenary inspiration: Scripture is theopneustos, breathed out by God through holy men borne along by the Holy Ghost, true and without error in all it affirms. Because God is its ultimate Author, the Scripture cannot be broken. The 1689 Confession grounds the whole authority of the Bible "wholly upon God, the author thereof"—to deny inspiration is to silence the voice of God and enthrone the autonomous critic in His place. Sola scriptura stands or falls here.

Hebrew Roots

Inspiration centers on the God-breathed character of the written Word.

expand to see more

Greek theopneustos — God-breathed; the one word behind 2 Timothy 3:16.

Greek pherō (as pheromenoi) — borne along, carried, as a ship by the wind (2 Pet 1:21).

Latin inspirare — to breathe into; source of the English "inspiration."

Verbal plenary inspiration — extending to the very words (verbal) and to every part (plenary).

Inspiration secures inerrancy and undergirds the doctrine of sola scriptura.

Usage

"Doctrinally, inspiration is the foundation of biblical authority, inerrancy, and sufficiency."

"Apologetically, it answers the historical-critical reduction of Scripture to mere human literature."

"Pastorally, it teaches the saint to receive every word of the Bible as the voice of God."
